newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN businessmen call for more easing of controls.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN businessmen call for more easing of controls.

text.p: A leading southeast Asian businessman said on Thursday that greater integration of the private sector in the region required even more loosening of government controls than had been planned.

Aburizal Bakrie, president of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told reporters on the fringes of a business summit that a target date of 2003 for an ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) was distant.

"My question is, are we going to wait until 2003? Are we going to do it (integrate the private sector) now? If we are going to do it now, we need some cooperation from the governments," he said. "They should lower their tariffs."

Bakrie was responding to a call by Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz on Wednesday that businesses in the region should take the cue from efforts by governments to set up a borderless economy in ASEAN.
She had suggested setting up ASEAN conglomerates that could take advantage of complementary businesses in the region to make inroads into the global economy.
"Such consortia, with the requisite capital and synergistic strength, can and will attract the large international players as partners," Aziz told the meeting.
Some 600 business leaders from 30 countries, including about 200 from the United States, are attending the two-day summit between ASEAN and its trading partners, which began on Wednesday.
ASEAN comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei. Cambodia, Laos and Burma are expected to join the bloc this year.

Participants have said that with the adoption of AFTA by 2003 and liberalisation of trade between Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) countries by 2020, the region should record explosive growth in the early part of the 21st century.
They said southeast Asia should have one billion consumers and $2.0 trillion in combined gross domestic product by 2020, up from the current 400 million and about $600 billion respectively.
Bakrie said more needed to be done.
"The ASEAN market should be opened at least for the projects which are already under AICO (the ASEAN Industrial Cooperation scheme)," he said.

AICO is a fast-track version of the AFTA proposals to reduce tariffs to between 0-5 percent by 2003, under which companies from two ASEAN countries can apply for reduced tariffs for products manufacured by a joint venture.
But the reduced tariffs will apply only to the two countries concerned, and Bakrie said AICO should be expanded to all ASEAN nations for non-sensitive products.
Other participants at the summit said that even under the current plans, ASEAN would become more attractive in years to come.

Kenneth Brown, General Electric's vice-president for southeast Asia, said his company's revenues from the region, which came to $3.4 billion in 1996 out of a total of $80 billion, would double by the turn of the century.
"The share of revenue from Asia in our total revenue is 10 percent while Asia's share of the global economy is 26 percent," he told reporters. "That gap is an opportunity for us."
